newsitem.title: USA: Optical Cable sees Q4 EPS $0.06-$0.07.
newsitem.headline: Optical Cable sees Q4 EPS $0.06-$0.07.

text.p: Optical Cable Corp said the company expected to report earnings of between $0.06 and $0.07 per share for the fourth quarter ended October 31.

That would represent year-over-year growth of 40 to 45 percent on a pro forma basis as if the company had been taxed in 1995 fiscal fourth-quarter as a publicly traded company, it said. The company underwrote its own public offering in April.

Robert Kopstein, Optical Cable's chairman and chief executive, said in a telephone interview that he remained comfortable with the company's previous earnings forecasts through the end of the 1999 fiscal year.
Optical plans to issue its latest quarterly earnings in the last week of December or the first week of January. "We're waiting for the accountants to sign off," Kopstein said.

Kopstein said Optical's decision to forecast earnings over the next three years was based on the absence of published research by Wall Street analysts on the company. The executive said he felt obliged to keep investors informed about his company's prospects.

"We are still in the middle of working with analysts who may pick up coverage of the company," Kopstein said. "Until those kind of reports are availabile, we feel we are obligated to present some picture until analysts will do it."
"People think we are doing a lot of hype, but people need the information," Kopstein said.
He said the company expected to report earnings for the fiscal 1996 year of between $0.19 and $0.20 per share on sales of about $45.2 million.

Optical had previously said it expected earnings in fiscal 1997 of $0.31 per share on sales of $62.7 million, growing in fiscal 1998 to $0.45 a share on sales of $91.5 million and in fiscal 1999 to $0.69 a share on sales of $136.8 million.
The executive said those estimates were based on overall industry growth trends in the optical fiber business and growth rates for the particular segments in which it operates.

Optical Cable's main business involves supplying fiber for use in local area networks used in data communications within office buidlings and campus locations. It does not extend to long-haul, city-to-city fiber telecommunications networks.
"Whatever other businesses we get in would be additional potential," Kopstein said. "I will leave it to Wall Street analysts to estimate what the potential upside might be."

He said possible markets include the use of fiber optic cable to build so-called "intelligent highway" systems, in which fiber cable would be installed at traffic signal intersections. Fiber optic sensors could be put to use in monitoring operations at refinery installations, he added.
